claim: Fusarium oxysporum ranks within the top 10 important fungal pathogens in terms of scientific and economic importance.
source: It ranks within the top 10 important fungal pathogens in terms of scientific and economic importance (Dean et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dean et al., 2012

claim: Currently, 14 SIX effectors have been identified in Fol consisting of small (less than 300 amino acids in length), secreted, cysteine-rich proteins.
source: Currently, 14 SIX effectors have been identified in Fol consisting of small (less than 300 amino acids in length), secreted, cysteine-rich proteins (Houterman et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2010; Rep et al., 2004; Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Most SIX effectors are encoded on the conditionally dispensable chromosome 14 required for Fol pathogenicity.
source: Most SIX effectors are encoded on the conditionally dispensable chromosome 14 required for Fol pathogenicity (Vlaardingerbroek et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vlaardingerbroek et al., 2016

claim: The dispensable chromosome can be horizontally transferred from Fol to a non-pathogenic strain of F. oxysporum, resulting in a transfer of pathogenicity.
source: This dispensable chromosome can be horizontally transferred from Fol to a non-pathogenic strain of F. oxysporum, resulting in a transfer of pathogenicity (Ma et al., 2010; Vlaardingerbroek et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2010 and Vlaardingerbroek et al., 2016

claim: All 14 SIX effectors lack sequence identity with proteins of known function.
source: To date, all 14 SIX effectors lack sequence identity with proteins of known function, preventing prediction of function based on their amino acid sequence.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge regarding SIX effectors

claim: SIX1, SIX2, SIX3, SIX5, and SIX6 from Fol have been shown to be essential for full virulence.
source: Several SIX effectors have been shown to be essential for full virulence, including SIX1, SIX2, SIX3, SIX5, and SIX6 from Fol (Rep et al., 2004; Gawehns et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2015; van der Does et al., 2008; Gawehns et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published studies

claim: Fol SIX3 (Avr2) and SIX5 are adjacent, divergently transcribed genes with a common promoter.
source: Fol SIX3 (Avr2) and SIX5 are adjacent, divergently transcribed genes with a common promoter, and SIX5 has been shown to interact with SIX3 to promote virulence by enabling symplastic movement of SIX3 via plasmodesmata (Cao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cao et al., 2018

claim: SIX5 interacts with SIX3 to promote virulence by enabling symplastic movement of SIX3 via plasmodesmata.
source: Fol SIX3 (Avr2) and SIX5 are adjacent, divergently transcribed genes with a common promoter, and SIX5 has been shown to interact with SIX3 to promote virulence by enabling symplastic movement of SIX3 via plasmodesmata (Cao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cao et al., 2018

claim: Focn SIX8 and PSE1 are divergently transcribed effector gene pairs that function together to suppress phytoalexin production and plant immunity in Arabidopsis.
source: Focn SIX8 and PSE1 (pair with SIX8 1) are also a divergently transcribed effector gene pair that function together to suppress phytoalexin production and plant immunity in Arabidopsis (Ayukawa et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ayukawa et al., 2021

claim: In Fol, SIX8 forms a similar gene pair with PSL1 (PSE1-like 1).
source: In Fol, SIX8 forms a similar gene pair with PSL1 (PSE1-like 1) (Ayukawa et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ayukawa et al., 2021

claim: I and I-7 encode transmembrane receptor proteins containing extracellular leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domains and short cytoplasmic domains (LRR-RPs).
source: I and I-7 encode transmembrane receptor proteins containing extracellular leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domains and short cytoplasmic domains (LRR-RPs) (Gonzalez-Cendales et al., 2016; Catanzariti et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gonzalez-Cendales et al., 2016 and Catanzariti et al., 2017

claim: I-2 encodes a cytoplasmic receptor containing nucleotide binding (NB) and C-terminal LRR domains.
source: I-2 encodes a cytoplasmic receptor containing nucleotide binding (NB) and C-terminal LRR domains (Simons et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to Simons et al., 1998

claim: I-3 encodes a transmembrane protein with an extracellular S-receptor-like domain and cytoplasmic serine/threonine kinase domain (SRLK).
source: I-3 encodes a transmembrane protein with an extracellular S-receptor-like domain and cytoplasmic serine/threonine kinase domain (SRLK) (Catanzariti et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Catanzariti et al., 2015

claim: Fol Avr1 (SIX4), Avr2 (SIX3), and Avr3 (SIX1) are recognised by tomato immunity receptors, I, I-2, and I-3, respectively, leading to effector-triggered immunity (ETI) and disease resistance.
source: Fol Avr1 (SIX4), Avr2 (SIX3), and Avr3 (SIX1) are recognised by tomato immunity receptors, I, I-2, and I-3, respectively, leading to effector-triggered immunity (ETI) and disease resistance (Rep et al., 2004; Houterman et al., 2008; Houterman et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rep et al., 2004, Houterman et al., 2008, and Houterman et al., 2009

claim: Avr2 represents the only SIX effector whose protein structure has been determined.
source: Currently, Avr2 represents the only SIX effector whose protein structure has been determined (Di et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Di et al., 2017 and statement about current state of knowledge

claim: The β-sandwich fold of Avr2 shares structural homology to ToxA from Pyrenophora tritici-repentis and AvrL567 from Melampsora lini, despite a lack of sequence identity.
source: Interestingly, the β-sandwich fold of Avr2 revealed that this effector shares structural homology to ToxA from Pyrenophora tritici-repentis and AvrL567 from Melampsora lini (Sarma et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2007), despite a lack of sequence identity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Sarma et al., 2005 and Wang et al., 2007

claim: Avr1 and Avr3 are cysteine-rich effectors that belong to the K2PP (Kex2-processed pro-domain) effector class.
source: Avr1 and Avr3 are cysteine-rich effectors that belong to the K2PP (Kex2-processed pro-domain) effector class (Outram et al., 2021b; Outram et al., 2021a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Outram et al., 2021b and Outram et al., 2021a

claim: The crystal structures of Avr1 and Avr3 were solved using a bromide-ion-based single-wavelength anomalous diffraction (SAD) approach.
source: The crystal structures of Avr1 and Avr3 were solved using a bromide-ion-based single-wavelength anomalous diffraction (SAD) approach (Supplementary file 1) and subsequently refined using a native dataset to a resolution of 1.65 Å and 1.68 Å, respectively (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Description of experimental methodology used in this study

claim: The crystal structure of Avr1 was refined to a resolution of 1.65 Å.
source: The crystal structures of Avr1 and Avr3 were solved using a bromide-ion-based single-wavelength anomalous diffraction (SAD) approach (Supplementary file 1) and subsequently refined using a native dataset to a resolution of 1.65 Å and 1.68 Å, respectively (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Experimental data from crystal structure determination

claim: The crystal structure of Avr3 was refined to a resolution of 1.68 Å.
source: The crystal structures of Avr1 and Avr3 were solved using a bromide-ion-based single-wavelength anomalous diffraction (SAD) approach (Supplementary file 1) and subsequently refined using a native dataset to a resolution of 1.65 Å and 1.68 Å, respectively (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Experimental data from crystal structure determination

claim: Avr1 and Avr3 share 19.5% amino-acid sequence identity.
source: Despite sharing low amino-acid sequence identity (19.5%), Avr1 and Avr3 adopt a structurally similar dual-domain protein fold.
evidence: Sequence comparison analysis performed in this study

claim: Avr1 and Avr3 adopt a structurally similar dual-domain protein fold despite sharing low amino-acid sequence identity.
source: Despite sharing low amino-acid sequence identity (19.5%), Avr1 and Avr3 adopt a structurally similar dual-domain protein fold.
evidence: Structural comparison based on experimentally determined crystal structures

claim: Interpretable, continuous electron density was observed from residue 96 in Avr3.
source: Interpretable, continuous electron density was observed from residue 96 in Avr3 and some regions of the intact pro-domain could be interpreted in the electron density (residues 26–49) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Observation from crystal structure electron density maps

claim: Some regions of the intact pro-domain of Avr3 could be interpreted in the electron density (residues 26–49).
source: Interpretable, continuous electron density was observed from residue 96 in Avr3 and some regions of the intact pro-domain could be interpreted in the electron density (residues 26–49) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Observation from crystal structure electron density maps

claim: An association between respective Avr and pro-domain was maintained post cleavage in vitro.
source: This indicates that an association between respective Avr and pro-domain was maintained post cleavage in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Inference from observation of pro-domain in crystal structure despite cleavage

claim: The Avr1 and Avr3 N-terminal domain (N-domain) consists of an N-terminal α-helix followed by five β-strands.
source: The Avr1 and Avr3 N-terminal domain (N-domain), consisting of an N-terminal α-helix followed by five β-strands, and C-terminal domain (C-domain), consisting of a β-sandwich architecture, involving seven or eight β-strands are very similar with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 2.1 Å and 2.8 Å, respectively (superposition performed using DALI server; Holm, 2022; Figure 1).
evidence: Structural analysis of experimentally determined crystal structures

claim: The Avr1 and Avr3 C-terminal domain (C-domain) consists of a β-sandwich architecture, involving seven or eight β-strands.
source: The Avr1 and Avr3 N-terminal domain (N-domain), consisting of an N-terminal α-helix followed by five β-strands, and C-terminal domain (C-domain), consisting of a β-sandwich architecture, involving seven or eight β-strands are very similar with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 2.1 Å and 2.8 Å, respectively (superposition performed using DALI server; Holm, 2022; Figure 1).
evidence: Structural analysis of experimentally determined crystal structures

claim: The N-domains of Avr1 and Avr3 are very similar with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 2.1 Å.
source: The Avr1 and Avr3 N-terminal domain (N-domain), consisting of an N-terminal α-helix followed by five β-strands, and C-terminal domain (C-domain), consisting of a β-sandwich architecture, involving seven or eight β-strands are very similar with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 2.1 Å and 2.8 Å, respectively (superposition performed using DALI server; Holm, 2022; Figure 1).
evidence: Structural comparison using DALI server

claim: The C-domains of Avr1 and Avr3 are very similar with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 2.8 Å.
source: The Avr1 and Avr3 N-terminal domain (N-domain), consisting of an N-terminal α-helix followed by five β-strands, and C-terminal domain (C-domain), consisting of a β-sandwich architecture, involving seven or eight β-strands are very similar with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 2.1 Å and 2.8 Å, respectively (superposition performed using DALI server; Holm, 2022; Figure 1).
evidence: Structural comparison using DALI server

claim: Superposition of the dual-domain structures of Avr1 and Avr3 returns an RMSD of ~3.4 Å.
source: While the individual domains are very similar, superposition of the dual-domain structures returns an RMSD of ~3.4 Å.
evidence: Structural comparison analysis

claim: The larger RMSD difference between full structures of Avr1 and Avr3 is due to a rotation between the N- and C-domains.
source: The larger difference is due to a rotation between the N- and C-domains (Figure 1E).
evidence: Inference from structural comparison

claim: Avr1 and Avr3 adopt a unique two-domain fold and represent the founding members of a new structural class of fungal effectors designated the FOLD effectors.
source: The structures of Avr1 and Avr3, when compared with the solved structures of other fungal effectors, demonstrate that they adopt a unique two-domain fold and represent the founding members of a new structural class of fungal effectors we have designated the FOLD effectors.
evidence: Conclusion based on structural comparison with known effector structures

claim: SIX6 and SIX13 contain a cysteine profile like Avr1 and Avr3.
source: We analysed the cysteine spacing of the other SIX effectors and found that SIX6 and SIX13 contained a cysteine profile like Avr1 and Avr3 (Figure 2A), suggesting that they may be FOLD effectors.
evidence: Sequence analysis performed in this study

claim: The cysteine profile similarity between SIX6, SIX13, Avr1, and Avr3 suggests that SIX6 and SIX13 may be FOLD effectors.
source: We analysed the cysteine spacing of the other SIX effectors and found that SIX6 and SIX13 contained a cysteine profile like Avr1 and Avr3 (Figure 2A), suggesting that they may be FOLD effectors.
evidence: Inference from sequence analysis

claim: The AlphaFold2 model of Avr1 returned a low average per-residue confidence score (pLDDT = 55%).
source: The AlphaFold2 model of Avr1 returned a low average per-residue confidence score (pLDDT = 55%) and the RMSD was 6.9 Å when model and structure were compared; however, the dual domain architecture was correctly predicted with a Z-score of 11.3 identified using a DALI pairwise structural comparison (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and E).
evidence: AlphaFold2 prediction results

claim: The RMSD between the AlphaFold2 model and crystal structure of Avr1 was 6.9 Å.
source: The AlphaFold2 model of Avr1 returned a low average per-residue confidence score (pLDDT = 55%) and the RMSD was 6.9 Å when model and structure were compared; however, the dual domain architecture was correctly predicted with a Z-score of 11.3 identified using a DALI pairwise structural comparison (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and E).
evidence: Comparison between AlphaFold2 model and experimental structure

claim: The dual domain architecture of Avr1 was correctly predicted by AlphaFold2 with a Z-score of 11.3.
source: The AlphaFold2 model of Avr1 returned a low average per-residue confidence score (pLDDT = 55%) and the RMSD was 6.9 Å when model and structure were compared; however, the dual domain architecture was correctly predicted with a Z-score of 11.3 identified using a DALI pairwise structural comparison (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and E).
evidence: Structural comparison between AlphaFold2 model and experimental structure

claim: The AlphaFold2 model of Avr3 returned a high average pLDDT score (92%).
source: The AlphaFold2 model of Avr3 returned a high average pLDDT score (92%) and superimposed well to the solved structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), despite a slight skew between the orientation of the individual domains (RMSD = 3.6 Å overall; 1.1 Å for the N-domain; 0.8 Å for the C-domain).
evidence: AlphaFold2 prediction results

claim: The AlphaFold2 model of Avr3 superimposed well to the solved structure with an overall RMSD of 3.6 Å.
source: The AlphaFold2 model of Avr3 returned a high average pLDDT score (92%) and superimposed well to the solved structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), despite a slight skew between the orientation of the individual domains (RMSD = 3.6 Å overall; 1.1 Å for the N-domain; 0.8 Å for the C-domain).
evidence: Comparison between AlphaFold2 model and experimental structure

claim: The RMSD between the AlphaFold2 model and crystal structure of Avr3 N-domain was 1.1 Å.
source: The AlphaFold2 model of Avr3 returned a high average pLDDT score (92%) and superimposed well to the solved structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), despite a slight skew between the orientation of the individual domains (RMSD = 3.6 Å overall; 1.1 Å for the N-domain; 0.8 Å for the C-domain).
evidence: Comparison between AlphaFold2 model and experimental structure

claim: The RMSD between the AlphaFold2 model and crystal structure of Avr3 C-domain was 0.8 Å.
source: The AlphaFold2 model of Avr3 returned a high average pLDDT score (92%) and superimposed well to the solved structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), despite a slight skew between the orientation of the individual domains (RMSD = 3.6 Å overall; 1.1 Å for the N-domain; 0.8 Å for the C-domain).
evidence: Comparison between AlphaFold2 model and experimental structure

claim: Accurate FOLD effector prediction is possible using AlphaFold2.
source: This demonstrated that accurate FOLD effector prediction was possible using AlphaFold2.
evidence: Conclusion based on comparison of AlphaFold2 models with experimental structures

claim: The SIX6 crystals diffracted X-rays to ~1.9 Å.
source: While the SIX13 crystals diffracted poorly, the SIX6 crystals diffracted X-rays to ~1.9 Å, and we solved the structure of SIX6 using the AlphaFold2-generated model as a template for molecular replacement (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1), confirming its inclusion as a member of the FOLD family.
evidence: Experimental data from X-ray crystallography

claim: The structure of SIX6 was solved using the AlphaFold2-generated model as a template for molecular replacement.
source: While the SIX13 crystals diffracted poorly, the SIX6 crystals diffracted X-rays to ~1.9 Å, and we solved the structure of SIX6 using the AlphaFold2-generated model as a template for molecular replacement (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1), confirming its inclusion as a member of the FOLD family.
evidence: Description of experimental methodology

claim: The SIX6 structure confirms its inclusion as a member of the FOLD family.
source: While the SIX13 crystals diffracted poorly, the SIX6 crystals diffracted X-rays to ~1.9 Å, and we solved the structure of SIX6 using the AlphaFold2-generated model as a template for molecular replacement (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1), confirming its inclusion as a member of the FOLD family.
evidence: Structural analysis of experimentally determined structure

claim: The SIX6 N-domain contains five β-strands held together by three disulfide bonds with an arrangement identical to Avr1 and Avr3.
source: Despite lacking an N-terminal helix, the N-domain contains five β-strands held together by three disulfide bonds with an arrangement, identical to Avr1 and Avr3.
evidence: Structural analysis of experimentally determined SIX6 structure

claim: The SIX6 C-domain is an eight stranded β-sandwich that is stabilised by a single disulfide bond connecting the β7 and β12 strands.
source: The C-domain is an eight stranded β-sandwich that is stabilised by a single disulfide bond (unique to SIX6 compared to Avr1 and Avr3) connecting the β7 and β12 strands.
evidence: Structural analysis of experimentally determined SIX6 structure

claim: The disulfide bond connecting the β7 and β12 strands in SIX6 C-domain is unique to SIX6 compared to Avr1 and Avr3.
source: The C-domain is an eight stranded β-sandwich that is stabilised by a single disulfide bond (unique to SIX6 compared to Avr1 and Avr3) connecting the β7 and β12 strands.
evidence: Structural comparison between SIX6, Avr1, and Avr3

claim: Regions of the pro-domain (residues 29–46) were identified within the SIX6 structure, despite cleavage of the pro-domain prior to crystallisation.
source: Like Avr1, we identified regions of the pro-domain within the SIX6 structure (residues 29–46), despite cleavage of the pro-domain prior to crystallisation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), but only within one molecule in the asymmetric unit (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Observation from crystal structure electron density maps

claim: The FOLD effectors share 15.5–22.5% sequence identities between all members.
source: Despite structural similarities, the FOLD effectors are divergent in their amino acid sequences, sharing 15.5–22.5% sequence identities between all members (Figure 2A).
evidence: Sequence comparison analysis

claim: Homologues of FOLD effectors are dispersed across multiple formae speciales of F. oxysporum.
source: Homologues of FOLD effectors are dispersed across multiple formae speciales of F. oxysporum (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Schmidt et al., 2013; Gawehns et al., 2014; Batson et al., 2021; Czislowski et al., 2018; Lievens et al., 2009; van Dam et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations and sequence analysis

claim: Structural-based searches using Avr1 and Avr3 as templates found three candidates predicted to be FOLD effectors in Venturia inaequalis.
source: Previous structural-based searches performed on effector candidates from Venturia inaequalis using Avr1 and Avr3 as templates (which we provided to the authors) found three candidates predicted to be FOLD effectors (Rocafort et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rocafort et al., 2022

claim: 124 putative FOLD protein family members were identified across three divisions of fungi (Ascomycota, Basidiomycota, and Glomeromycota).
source: This analysis identified 124 putative FOLD protein family members across three divisions of fungi (Ascomycota, Basidiomycota, and Glomeromycota) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Results from Foldseek webserver search

claim: Over half of the putative FOLD protein family members were found in Ascomycota fungi (73).
source: Over half of these were found in Ascomycota fungi (73), with expanded families in species of Fusarium and Colletotrichum (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Results from Foldseek webserver search

claim: Expanded families of FOLD proteins were observed in species of Fusarium and Colletotrichum.
source: Over half of these were found in Ascomycota fungi (73), with expanded families in species of Fusarium and Colletotrichum (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Results from Foldseek webserver search

claim: Expanded families of FOLD proteins were observed in the division Glomeromycota that form arbuscular mycorrhiza in plant roots.
source: Expanded families of FOLD proteins were also observed in the division Glomeromycota that form arbuscular mycorrhiza in plant roots, while two putative FOLD effectors were also predicted in the ectomycorrhizal fungus Piloderma olivaceum (division Basidiomycota), which forms mutualistic associations with conifer and hardwood species (van Kempen et al., 2023).
evidence: Results from Foldseek webserver search

claim: Two putative FOLD effectors were predicted in the ectomycorrhizal fungus Piloderma olivaceum (division Basidiomycota).
source: Expanded families of FOLD proteins were also observed in the division Glomeromycota that form arbuscular mycorrhiza in plant roots, while two putative FOLD effectors were also predicted in the ectomycorrhizal fungus Piloderma olivaceum (division Basidiomycota), which forms mutualistic associations with conifer and hardwood species (van Kempen et al., 2023).
evidence: Results from Foldseek webserver search

claim: The major differences identified between FOLD effectors from different fungal divisions are the orientation of the domains relative to each other.
source: Structural superposition of members from the three divisions confirms the structural similarities between the N and C domains and highlights that the major differences identified are the orientation of the domains relative to each other (Figure 2D), consistent with our experimental data for Avr1, Avr3 and SIX6.
evidence: Structural comparison analysis

claim: The observed structural similarity between the FOLD effectors was high, with Z-scores above 8 for all comparisons.
source: The observed structural similarity between the FOLD effectors was high, with Z-scores above 8 for all comparisons (Figure 3A).
evidence: Structural comparison using DALI server

claim: Avr2 exhibited structural similarity with the SIX7 and SIX8 models (Z-scores > 5).
source: Avr2, a member of the ToxA-like effector family, exhibited structural similarity with the SIX7 and SIX8 models (Z-scores > 5) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Structural comparison using DALI server

claim: SIX7 and SIX8 both consist of a β-sandwich fold, strongly indicating their inclusion within the ToxA-like structural family.
source: Analysis of the models and topology show that SIX7 and SIX8 both consist of a β-sandwich fold, strongly indicating their inclusion within the ToxA-like structural family (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Structural analysis of AlphaFold2 models

claim: SIX9 and SIX11 form structural family 3.
source: Here, we define these as structural family 3 and 4, consisting of SIX9 and SIX11, and SIX5 and SIX14, respectively (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Classification based on structural comparison

claim: SIX5 and SIX14 form structural family 4.
source: Here, we define these as structural family 3 and 4, consisting of SIX9 and SIX11, and SIX5 and SIX14, respectively (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Classification based on structural comparison

claim: The models of SIX9 and SIX11 both consist of five β-strands and either two or three α-helices.
source: The models of SIX9 and SIX11 both consist of five β-strands and either two or three α-helices (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), despite sharing only 14% sequence identity.
evidence: Structural analysis of AlphaFold2 models

claim: SIX9 and SIX11 share only 14% sequence identity.
source: The models of SIX9 and SIX11 both consist of five β-strands and either two or three α-helices (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), despite sharing only 14% sequence identity.
evidence: Sequence comparison analysis

claim: Both SIX9 and SIX11 structures share structural similarity to various RNA-binding proteins (Z-scores > 2.5).
source: To further our understanding of the putative function of this family, we did a structural search against the protein databank (PDB) and found that both structures share structural similarity to various RNA-binding proteins (Z-scores > 2.5), such as the RNA recognition motif (RRM) fold of the Musashi-1 RNA-binding domain (PDB code: 5X3Z) (Iwaoka et al., 2017) with Z-scores of 2.6 and 4.5 for SIX9 and SIX11, respectively.
evidence: Structural comparison against PDB using DALI

claim: SIX9 has a Z-score of 2.6 with the RNA recognition motif (RRM) fold of the Musashi-1 RNA-binding domain.
source: To further our understanding of the putative function of this family, we did a structural search against the protein databank (PDB) and found that both structures share structural similarity to various RNA-binding proteins (Z-scores > 2.5), such as the RNA recognition motif (RRM) fold of the Musashi-1 RNA-binding domain (PDB code: 5X3Z) (Iwaoka et al., 2017) with Z-scores of 2.6 and 4.5 for SIX9 and SIX11, respectively.
evidence: Structural comparison against PDB

claim: SIX11 has a Z-score of 4.5 with the RNA recognition motif (RRM) fold of the Musashi-1 RNA-binding domain.
source: To further our understanding of the putative function of this family, we did a structural search against the protein databank (PDB) and found that both structures share structural similarity to various RNA-binding proteins (Z-scores > 2.5), such as the RNA recognition motif (RRM) fold of the Musashi-1 RNA-binding domain (PDB code: 5X3Z) (Iwaoka et al., 2017) with Z-scores of 2.6 and 4.5 for SIX9 and SIX11, respectively.
evidence: Structural comparison against PDB

claim: SIX5 and SIX14 share limited sequence identity (23%).
source: SIX5 and SIX14 also share limited sequence identity (23%) but the structural predictions show a similar secondary-structure topology consisting of 2 α-helices and 4–6 β-strands (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Sequence comparison analysis

claim: The structural predictions of SIX5 and SIX14 show a similar secondary-structure topology consisting of 2 α-helices and 4–6 β-strands.
source: SIX5 and SIX14 also share limited sequence identity (23%) but the structural predictions show a similar secondary-structure topology consisting of 2 α-helices and 4–6 β-strands (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Structural analysis of AlphaFold2 models

claim: The models of SIX5 and SIX14 have structural similarity toward the Ustilago maydis and Zymoseptoria tritici KP6 effector, suggesting that SIX5 and SIX14 belong to the KP6-like structural family.
source: We compared the models of SIX5 and SIX14 against the PDB using DALI and identified structural similarity toward the Ustilago maydis and Zymoseptoria tritici KP6 effector (PDB codes: 4GVB and 6QPK) (Allen et al., 2013), suggesting that SIX5 and SIX14 belong to the KP6-like structural family (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Structural comparison against PDB using DALI

claim: 11 of the 14 SIX effectors group into four different structural families.
source: Collectively, this analysis demonstrates that 11 of the 14 SIX effectors group into four different structural families.
evidence: Summary of structural classification analysis

claim: A total of 26 genes encoding novel effector candidates were identified that were consistently upregulated during Fol infection.
source: A total of 26 genes encoding novel effector candidates were identified that were consistently upregulated during Fol infection (Sun et al., 2022), which were not previously predicted or predicted incorrectly in the original genome annotation (Ma et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2022

claim: 14 of the 26 novel effector candidate genes encoded proteins with no recognised domains or motifs based on their amino acid sequences.
source: Of these, 14 genes encoded proteins with no recognised domains or motifs based on their amino acid sequences.
evidence: Sequence analysis of effector candidates

claim: The predicted structure of FOXGR_015533 adopts a nine β-stranded sandwich and is likely a member of the ToxA-like class.
source: We found that the predicted structure of FOXGR_015533 adopts a nine β-stranded sandwich and is likely a member of the ToxA-like class (Figure 3C).
evidence: Structural analysis of AlphaFold2 model

claim: PSL1 and FOXGR_015322 (designated PSL2) are sequence-related effectors (~85% sequence identity) and show a conserved structure.
source: PSL1 (Ayukawa et al., 2021) and FOXGR_015322, here designated PSL2, are sequence-related effectors (~85% sequence identity) and show a conserved structure (Figure 3E).
evidence: Sequence comparison and structural analysis

claim: PSL1 and PSL2 have Z-scores of >2 against family 4 and are likely members of this family.
source: Both have Z-scores of >2 against family 4 and are likely members of this family.
evidence: Structural comparison using DALI

claim: FOXG_18699 and FOXGR_015522 are structurally related (Z-score of 2.2) with a sequence identity of ~29%.
source: FOXG_18699 and FOXGR_015522 are structurally related (Z-score of 2.2) with a sequence identity of ~29%.
evidence: Structural comparison and sequence analysis

claim: FOXG_18699 and FOXGR_015522 belong to an independent structural family, designated family 5.
source: While FOXGR_015522 does share some resemblance to family 4, based on manual alignment (Figure 3F) and domain topology analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), these effectors appear to belong to an independent structural family, designated family 5.
evidence: Structural analysis and manual alignment

claim: Fol utilises multiple structurally related, sequence-diverse, effectors during infection of tomato.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that Fol utilises multiple structurally related, sequence-diverse, effectors during infection of tomato.
evidence: Summary conclusion from structural analysis

claim: In Fol, Avr2 and SIX5, and SIX8 and PSL1 form a similar head-to-head relationship in the genome with shared promoters and are divergently-transcribed.
source: In Fol, Avr2 and SIX5, and SIX8 and PSL1 form a similar head-to-head relationship in the genome with shared promoters and are divergently-transcribed (Figure 4A; Cao et al., 2018; Ayukawa et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations and genomic analysis

claim: Avr2 and SIX5 function together and interact directly via yeast-two-hybrid analysis.
source: Previously, studies concerning Avr2 and SIX5 have demonstrated that the proteins function together and interact directly via yeast-two-hybrid analysis (Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma et al., 2015

claim: Homologues of SIX8 and PSL1 from Focn (SIX8 and PSE1) are functionally dependent on each other; however, an interaction could not be established in yeast.
source: Homologues of SIX8 and PSL1 from Focn (SIX8 and PSE1) are also functionally dependent on each other; however, an interaction could not be established in yeast (Ayukawa et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ayukawa et al., 2021

claim: Both protein pairs (Avr2/SIX5 and SIX8/PSL1) contain a ToxA-like family member and a structural family 4 member.
source: Here we demonstrate that both protein pairs contain a ToxA-like family member (Avr2, SIX8) and a structural family 4 member (SIX5, PSL1).
evidence: Conclusion from structural classification analysis

claim: The elution profile of PSL1 alone showed a major peak (~12.25 mL) at a volume consistent with a dimeric form of the protein.
source: The elution profile of PSL1 alone showed a major peak (~12.25 mL) at a volume consistent with a dimeric form of the protein, while SIX8 showed a major peak (~15 mL) consistent with a monomer (Figure 4B).
evidence: Experimental data from size-exclusion chromatography

claim: SIX8 showed a major peak (~15 mL) consistent with a monomer.
source: The elution profile of PSL1 alone showed a major peak (~12.25 mL) at a volume consistent with a dimeric form of the protein, while SIX8 showed a major peak (~15 mL) consistent with a monomer (Figure 4B).
evidence: Experimental data from size-exclusion chromatography

claim: When PSL1 and SIX8 were incubated together, the major protein peaks migrate to ~12.8 mL, indicating that the migration of both proteins on SEC is altered after incubation.
source: Strikingly, when incubated together the major protein peaks migrate to ~12.8 mL. SDS-PAGE analysis confirmed the presence of PSL1 and SIX8, indicating that the migration of both proteins on SEC is altered after incubation (Figure 4B).
evidence: Experimental data from size-exclusion chromatography and SDS-PAGE

claim: The SEC data are consistent with PSL1 and SIX8 forming a heterodimer.
source: These data are consistent with PSL1 and SIX8 forming a heterodimer.
evidence: Inference from SEC experimental data

claim: The thiol side chain of a free cysteine in PSL1 (Cys 37) and SIX8 (Cys 58) co-localised in the dimer interface in AlphaFold2-Multimer models.
source: Manual inspection of the top 5 models (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, top model shown in Figure 4C) demonstrated that the thiol side chain of a free cysteine in PSL1 (Cys 37) and SIX8 (Cys 58) co-localised in the dimer interface, suggesting that an inter-disulfide bond may mediate the interaction.
evidence: Analysis of AlphaFold2-Multimer models

claim: The co-localisation of Cys 37 in PSL1 and Cys 58 in SIX8 suggests that an inter-disulfide bond may mediate the interaction.
source: Manual inspection of the top 5 models (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, top model shown in Figure 4C) demonstrated that the thiol side chain of a free cysteine in PSL1 (Cys 37) and SIX8 (Cys 58) co-localised in the dimer interface, suggesting that an inter-disulfide bond may mediate the interaction.
evidence: Inference from AlphaFold2-Multimer models

claim: The mass observed from the incubated SIX8 and PSL1 non-reduced sample contained a predominant species consistent with the combined molecular weight of SIX8 and PSL1 (20,777 Da).
source: The mass observed from the incubated SIX8 and PSL1 non-reduced sample contained a predominant species consistent with the combined molecular weight of SIX8 and PSL1 (20,777 Da) (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2G and H).
evidence: Experimental data from intact mass spectrometry

claim: SIX8 and PSL1 failed to form a heterodimer with an unrelated protein containing a free cysteine, suggesting specificity in the interaction.
source: SIX8 and PSL1 failed to form a heterodimer with an unrelated protein containing a free cysteine, suggesting specificity in the interaction (Figure 4—figure supplements 2I and 3J–L).
evidence: Experimental data from mass spectrometry control experiments

claim: The SIX8-PSL1 heterodimer is mediated via a disulfide bond.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrated that the SIX8-PSL1 heterodimer is mediated via a disulfide bond.
evidence: Conclusion from mass spectrometry and SEC experiments

claim: The structure of SIX8_C58S was solved at 1.28 Å and confirms its inclusion within the ToxA-like structural family.
source: We crystallised and solved the structure of SIX8_C58S at 1.28 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) which confirms its inclusion within the ToxA-like structural family.
evidence: Experimental data from X-ray crystallography

claim: Co-expression of the I gene from the M82 tomato cultivar (IM82) with Avr1 in Nicotiana benthamiana leads to a cell death response.
source: Previous studies have shown co-expression of the I gene from the M82 tomato cultivar (IM82) with Avr1 in Nicotiana benthamiana leads to a cell death response, a proxy for ETI (Catanzariti et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Catanzariti et al., 2017

claim: Co-expression with the allelic variant (iMoneymaker) from the susceptible cultivar Moneymaker does not lead to cell death as the receptor cannot recognise Avr1.
source: Conversely, co-expression with the allelic variant (iMoneymaker) from the susceptible cultivar Moneymaker does not lead to cell death as the receptor cannot recognise Avr1 (Catanzariti et al., 2017; Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by citation and experimental data

claim: FonSIX4, a homologue of Avr1 from F. oxysporum f. sp. niveum (Fon), shares 79% identity with Avr1.
source: FonSIX4, a homologue of Avr1 from the watermelon pathogen, F. oxysporum f. sp. niveum (Fon), shares 79% identity with Avr1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Sequence comparison analysis

claim: FonSIX4 is recognised by I receptors from both cultivars (IM82 and iMoneymaker).
source: Using the N. benthamiana assay, we show FonSIX4 is recognised by I receptors from both cultivars (IM82 and iMoneymaker) and cell death is dependent on the presence of IM82 or iMoneymaker (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Experimental data from N. benthamiana assays

claim: Cell death induced by FonSIX4 is dependent on the presence of IM82 or iMoneymaker.
source: Using the N. benthamiana assay, we show FonSIX4 is recognised by I receptors from both cultivars (IM82 and iMoneymaker) and cell death is dependent on the presence of IM82 or iMoneymaker (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Experimental data from N. benthamiana assays

claim: FonSIX4 and Avr1 differ by 34 residues distributed across both N- and C-domains of the protein.
source: FonSIX4 and Avr1 differ by 34 residues distributed across both N- and C-domains of the protein (Figure 5A).
evidence: Sequence comparison analysis

claim: The C-domain of FonSIX4 is recognised by iMoneymaker.
source: When these were co-expressed with iMoneymaker, the cell death response, quantified using ion leakage assays (Figure 5D and E) and visual inspection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggests the C-domain of FonSIX4 is recognised by iMoneymaker.
evidence: Experimental data from N. benthamiana assays with chimeric proteins

claim: The C-domains of Avr1 and FonSIX4 are sufficient for I receptor recognition.
source: Quantification using ion leakage assays demonstrate that the C-domains of Avr1 and FonSIX4 cause cell death when expressed with IM82 and IM82/Moneymaker, respectively. These data confirm the C-domain is sufficient for I receptor recognition (Figure 5D and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for N. benthamiana leaf infiltration and protein accumulation data).
evidence: Experimental data from N. benthamiana assays with domain-separated proteins

claim: Avr1EEEYGIN showed consistent ion leakage and cell death similar to FonSIX4 when co-expressed with iMoneymaker.
source: Avr1EEEYGIN showed consistent ion leakage and cell death similar to FonSIX4 (Figure 5F and G), whereas ion leakage quantification for the other three mutants (Avr1ADVKT, Avr1IDH, Avr1NGQAR) was statistically similar to the non-recognised Avr1 (Figure 5G).
evidence: Experimental data from N. benthamiana assays with Avr1 mutants

claim: Ion leakage quantification for Avr1ADVKT, Avr1IDH, and Avr1NGQAR was statistically similar to the non-recognised Avr1.
source: Avr1EEEYGIN showed consistent ion leakage and cell death similar to FonSIX4 (Figure 5F and G), whereas ion leakage quantification for the other three mutants (Avr1ADVKT, Avr1IDH, Avr1NGQAR) was statistically similar to the non-recognised Avr1 (Figure 5G).
evidence: Experimental data from N. benthamiana assays with Avr1 mutants

claim: The reciprocal mutation FonSIX4KEVYHID significantly reduced ion leakage and cell death response when co-expressed with iMoneymaker compared to FonSIX4.
source: The reciprocal mutations in FonSIX4 (FonSIX4KEVYHID) significantly reduced ion leakage and cell death response when co-expressed with iMoneymaker compared to FonSIX4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E, see Figure 5—figure supplement 1G for protein accumulation data).
evidence: Experimental data from N. benthamiana assays with FonSIX4 mutants

claim: The C-domain in Avr1 is recognised by IM82.
source: Collectively, these data show that the C-domain in Avr1 is recognised by IM82, and surface-exposed residues in the C-domain allow Avr1 to escape recognition by iMoneymaker.
evidence: Conclusion from N. benthamiana assays with chimeric and mutant proteins

claim: Surface-exposed residues in the C-domain allow Avr1 to escape recognition by iMoneymaker.
source: Collectively, these data show that the C-domain in Avr1 is recognised by IM82, and surface-exposed residues in the C-domain allow Avr1 to escape recognition by iMoneymaker.
evidence: Conclusion from N. benthamiana assays with chimeric and mutant proteins

claim: The Fol SIX effectors can be classified into a reduced set of structural families despite their sequence diversity.
source: Here, we demonstrate that despite their sequence diversity, the Fol SIX effectors can be classified into a reduced set of structural families.
evidence: Summary conclusion from structural analysis

claim: Five fungal effector families have been defined based on experimentally determined structural homology, including the MAX, RALPH, ToxA-like, LARS, and FOLD effectors.
source: To date, five fungal effector families have been defined based on experimentally determined structural homology, including the MAX (de Guillen et al., 2015), RALPH (Spanu, 2017; Pennington et al., 2019; Pedersen et al., 2012), ToxA-like (Di et al., 2017; Sarma et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2007), LARS (Lazar et al., 2022; Blondeau et al., 2015), and FOLD effectors, defined here.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and this study

claim: The ToxA-like family includes effectors from fungi that group to both divisions of higher-fungi (Basidiomycota and Ascomycota fungi).
source: The ToxA-like family includes effectors from fungi that group to both divisions of higher-fungi (Basidiomycota and Ascomycota fungi) (Di et al., 2017; Sarma et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: The MAX effector family are widely distributed amongst the Dothideomycetes and Sordariomycetes.
source: The MAX effector family were originally defined as AVR effectors from M. oryzae and ToxB from P. tritici-repentis (de Guillen et al., 2015) but pattern-based sequence searches suggest they are widely distributed amongst the Dothideomycetes and Sordariomycetes (de Guillen et al., 2015; Petit-Houdenot et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: LARS effectors have structural homologues predicted in at least 13 different fungal species.
source: Similarly, LARS effectors, defined in Leptosphaeria maculans and Fulvia fulva, have structural homologues predicted in at least 13 different fungal species (Lazar et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lazar et al., 2022

claim: The exclusive presence of FOLD effectors in plant-colonising fungi may suggest that they facilitate plant colonisation in pathogenic and symbiotic fungi.
source: The exclusive presence of FOLD effectors in plant-colonising fungi may suggest that they facilitate plant colonisation in pathogenic and symbiotic fungi (Teulet et al., 2023).
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to Teulet et al., 2023

claim: The accuracy of models generated by AlphaFold2 can decline in cases with low numbers of homologues (~30 sequences in the multiple sequence alignment).
source: The accuracy of models generated by AlphaFold2 can decline in cases with low numbers of homologues (~30 sequences in the multiple sequence alignment [MSA]) (Jumper et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jumper et al., 2021

claim: The low-confidence prediction for SIX4 (Avr1) may be explained by it being only distributed in a few ff. spp. of F. oxysporum.
source: This may help explain the low-confidence prediction for SIX4 (Avr1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which is only distributed in a few ff. spp. of F. oxysporum.
evidence: Inference from AlphaFold2 prediction results and sequence distribution

claim: AlphaFold2 models were critical in solving the structure of SIX6 and SIX8 as templates for molecular replacement.
source: Despite this, AlphaFold2 models were critical in solving the structure of SIX6 and SIX8 as templates for molecular replacement.
evidence: Description of experimental methodology

claim: The N-domain of FOLD effectors have structural similarities with cystatin cysteine protease inhibitors.
source: However, at a domain level, the N-domain of FOLD effectors have structural similarities with cystatin cysteine protease inhibitors (PDB code: 4N6V; PDB code: 5ZC1) (Park et al., 2018; Renko et al., 2014), while the C-domains have structural similarities with tumour necrosis factors (PDB code: 6X83) (Dietrich et al., 2021) and carbohydrate-binding lectins (PDB code: 2WQ4) (Sulák et al., 2010).
evidence: Structural comparison against PDB with citations

claim: The C-domains of FOLD effectors have structural similarities with tumour necrosis factors and carbohydrate-binding lectins.
source: However, at a domain level, the N-domain of FOLD effectors have structural similarities with cystatin cysteine protease inhibitors (PDB code: 4N6V; PDB code: 5ZC1) (Park et al., 2018; Renko et al., 2014), while the C-domains have structural similarities with tumour necrosis factors (PDB code: 6X83) (Dietrich et al., 2021) and carbohydrate-binding lectins (PDB code: 2WQ4) (Sulák et al., 2010).
evidence: Structural comparison against PDB with citations

claim: The ToxA-like effectors, Avr2 and SIX8, form functional effector pairs with SIX5 and PSE1 (PSL1-homologue), respectively.
source: The ToxA-like effectors, Avr2 and SIX8, are known to form functional effector pairs with SIX5 and PSE1 (PSL1-homolouge), respectively (Ma et al., 2015; Ayukawa et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: SIX7 and SIX12 potentially share a common promoter as they possess start codons 2319 base-pairs apart.
source: SIX7 (ToxA-like family) and SIX12 possess start codons 2319 base-pairs apart and potentially share a common promoter.
evidence: Genomic analysis

claim: The cysteine spacing in SIX12 closely resembles other family 4 members, suggesting that SIX12 may also be a family 4 member.
source: On closer inspection of the sequence, we observed that the cysteine spacing in SIX12 closely resembles other family 4 members (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), which suggests that SIX12 may also be a family 4 member.
evidence: Sequence analysis

claim: SIX7 and SIX12 may function together, as described for the Avr2/SIX5 and SIX8/PSL1 pairs.
source: We therefore speculate that SIX7 and SIX12 may function together, as described for the Avr2/SIX5 and SIX8/PSL1 pairs.
evidence: Speculation based on structural and genomic similarities

claim: Different immunity receptor classes can recognise structural homologues.
source: This is significant because it demonstrates that different immunity receptor classes can recognise structural homologues.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental data showing I (LRR-RP) and I-3 (SRLK) recognise FOLD effectors

claim: AvrLm4-7 can prevent recognition of AvrLm3 and AvrLm9 (all LARS structural homologues) by their cognate Rlm receptors.
source: AvrLm4-7 can prevent recognition of AvrLm3 and AvrLm9 (all LARS structural homologues; Lazar et al., 2022), by their cognate Rlm receptors (Plissonneau et al., 2016; Ghanbarnia et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Members of at least two different structural effector families can suppress immunity triggered by structurally homologous effectors.
source: These studies demonstrate that members of at least two different structural effector families can suppress immunity triggered by structurally homologous effectors.
evidence: Conclusion from cited studies and this work
